meta.title: Ebola Tracker: DR Congo
meta.description: Independent, sourced tracker of the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in DR Congo: confirmed cases and deaths, affected provinces, spread to other countries, vaccines, WHO risk and a dated timeline.
meta.disclaimer: This tracker summarises WHO, CDC, ECDC, Africa CDC and national health ministry reports and named news outlets. It is not medical or travel advice. If you develop fever within 21 days of being in an affected area, call a doctor before going to a clinic.

headline: DR Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 8,700 confirmed cases and 4,200 deaths. Kenya reports its first imported case.

status.label: Growing · global health emergency
status.summary: The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak declared on 15 May has spread to 64 health zones in 7 of DR Congo's 26 provinces. ECDC, reporting DR Congo's data, counted 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 deaths as of 6 October; CDC calls it the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There is no licensed vaccine for this strain; trials of an existing Ebola vaccine began in August.

claims.claim: There is a vaccine for this Ebola strain
claims.detail: No vaccine is licensed for Bundibugyo virus. Ervebo, licensed for Zaire Ebola, is being tested in trials; whether it protects against Bundibugyo is unknown.

claims.claim: This is the largest Ebola outbreak ever
claims.detail: It is the largest ever in DR Congo and the second-largest on record. The 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak had about 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths.
CDC reports no confirmed US cases as of 2 October. Two US citizens infected in DR Congo were treated in Germany and recovered.

claims.claim: Ebola spreads through the air like measles or flu
claims.detail: It spreads through direct contact with the body fluids of a sick person or someone who died of it. People are not contagious before they have symptoms.
Kenya confirmed one imported case on 5 October; the patient, who had travelled from DR Congo via Kampala, died. No local spread has been reported.
Modelling cited by WHO's Emergency Committee suggests true infections may be three to four times the reported count. Africa CDC says contact tracing reaches only about a quarter of expected contacts.

positions.text: 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths in 63 health zones across 7 provinces. Risk very high in DR Congo, high for neighbouring countries, low globally. Still a Public Health Emergency of International Concern.
8,603 confirmed cases and 4,148 deaths in DR Congo; the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. No US cases.
8,067 confirmed cases and 3,901 deaths in 63 health zones of 7 provinces, as reported by AP.
Confirmed Kenya's first imported Bundibugyo case; the patient died. Contacts are being traced and followed.
The outbreak remains a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security, declared on 18 May.

timeline.title: First known case falls ill in Bunia
timeline.body: A health worker who later died in Bunia, Ituri province, is the earliest known case. Investigators believe the outbreak started in the Mongbwalu mining area.

timeline.title: WHO alerted to a deadly unknown illness in Ituri
timeline.body: Reports describe a high-mortality illness in Mongbwalu health zone, including four health workers who died within four days.

timeline.title: DR Congo and Uganda declare a Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak
timeline.body: The national lab confirms Bundibugyo virus. It is DR Congo's 17th Ebola outbreak. Uganda confirms a case in Kampala the same day.

timeline.title: WHO declares a global health emergency
timeline.body: The WHO Director-General declares a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, the first time this was done before convening an Emergency Committee.

timeline.title: Africa CDC declares a continental emergency; US restricts entry
timeline.body: Africa CDC declares a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security. The US suspends entry for foreign nationals recently in DR Congo, Uganda or South Sudan.

timeline.title: US$518 million response plan launched
timeline.body: Africa CDC and WHO launch a joint continental plan covering June to November 2026.

timeline.title: France reports an imported case
timeline.body: An intensive-care doctor returning from DR Congo tests positive in France. He recovers, and none of his contacts fall ill.

timeline.title: First treatment trial for Bundibugyo Ebola begins
timeline.body: The PARTNERS trial enrols its first patient, testing an antibody treatment and remdesivir.

timeline.title: Largest Ebola outbreak in DR Congo's history
timeline.body: With 3,605 confirmed cases in DR Congo, the outbreak passes the 2018–2020 North Kivu outbreak.

timeline.title: WHO keeps the global emergency in place
timeline.body: WHO's Emergency Committee meets for the second time. Modelling it cites suggests true infections may be three to four times the reported count.

timeline.title: Vaccination of health workers begins; Uganda declared Ebola-free
timeline.body: DR Congo starts giving Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for a different Ebola species, to health workers in trials. WHO and Africa CDC confirm the end of Uganda's outbreak after 42 days without cases.

timeline.title: Outbreak reaches a seventh province, Sud-Ubangi
timeline.body: A death in Bulu health zone marks the first spread to western DR Congo.

timeline.title: Frontline worker vaccine study launched in Bunia
timeline.body: MSF's BRAVO study plans to vaccinate about 20,000 frontline workers in Ituri and North Kivu.

timeline.title: WHO: 7,890 cases, 3,799 deaths in 63 health zones
timeline.body: The outbreak has reached Dungu health zone, on the border with South Sudan. WHO rates the risk very high in DR Congo and high for neighbouring countries.

timeline.title: G20 pledges more than US$470 million
timeline.body: New pledges at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting include US$267 million from the US.

timeline.title: MSF health worker evacuated to the Netherlands
timeline.body: A Medecins Sans Frontieres staff member infected in DR Congo is admitted to Leiden University Medical Center.

timeline.title: CDC: 8,442 cases and 4,080 deaths
timeline.body: CDC calls it the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record and says it is spreading faster than earlier ones. No cases in the US.

timeline.title: Kenya's first imported case dies in Nairobi
timeline.body: A Kenyan citizen living in DR Congo travelled by road to Kampala and flew to Nairobi on 3 October. He tested positive and died on 5 October. Contacts are being followed.

timeline.title: CDC and ECDC: 8,603 cases and 4,148 deaths
timeline.body: DR Congo's confirmed total reaches 8,603 cases, including 4,148 deaths, with data to 4 October. ECDC notes that DR Congo's figures are under continuous review and may be revised.

timeline.title: ECDC: 8,728 cases and 4,205 deaths
timeline.body: ECDC's update of 7 October, with data to 6 October, reports DR Congo's confirmed total at 8,728 cases, including 4,205 deaths. Ituri has 6,513 cases and North Kivu 1,785. ECDC notes that DR Congo's figures are under continuous review and may be revised.

history.text: Bundibugyo virus is first identified in Bundibugyo District, Uganda: 131 cases and 42 deaths.
Second known outbreak, around Isiro in north-eastern DR Congo.
The largest Bundibugyo outbreak by far: more than 8,400 confirmed cases in DR Congo, plus cases in Uganda, France and Kenya.

facts.a: Through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of a person who is sick with or has died from Ebola, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air, and people are not contagious before symptoms start.
Fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, rash and in some cases bleeding. Symptoms appear 2 to 21 days after infection, usually within 4 to 10.
There is no licensed treatment for Bundibugyo virus. Early supportive care improves survival. A trial testing an antibody treatment and remdesivir began in July 2026.
Not for this strain. Ervebo protects against Zaire Ebola; trials in DR Congo are testing whether it helps against Bundibugyo, starting with health and frontline workers.
It is one of several Ebola virus species, named after the district in Uganda where it was first identified in 2007. Fruit bats are the suspected natural host.
